ref_gdpr.overview: The General Data Protection Regulation (EU 2016/679) — the world's most influential data protection law and, until the AI Act, the EU's main lever over AI. For AI governance its pressure points are: lawful basis and purpose limitation for training data, Article 22's limits on solely automated decisions, Article 9's special-category rules, Article 35 DPIAs, data subject rights that reach into models, and Article 28's controller-processor contracting regime.
ref_gdpr.exam: The second-most-tested law after the AI Act. Anchor articles by number: 5 (principles), 6 (lawful bases), 9 (special categories), 13-15 (transparency/access), 17 (erasure), 22 (automated decisions), 25 (data protection by design), 28 (processors), 33-34 (breach notice), 35 (DPIA). Fines: up to €20M or 4% of global turnover.
key_points: Article 5 principles: lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, accountability

Article 22: right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects — exceptions (contract, law, explicit consent) require safeguards including human intervention
Article 35 DPIAs for likely-high-risk processing; consult the supervisory authority if risk remains high (Art 36)
Data subject rights vs. AI: access includes meaningful information about automated decision-making logic; erasure and objection extend to profiling
Breach regime: notify the DPA within 72 hours (Art 33); notify individuals when high risk (Art 34)
Penalties: two tiers — up to €10M/2% and up to €20M/4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
Extraterritorial scope (Art 3): applies to processing of EU residents' data by controllers anywhere when offering goods/services or monitoring behavior

ref_gpai_cop.overview: The Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI Models (2025), published under Article 56 of the EU AI Act by the European AI Office. It translates GPAI providers' statutory duties into concrete committed Measures across three chapters: Transparency (documentation, downstream information) and Copyright (TDM opt-out compliance, anti-infringement) for all providers, and Safety & Security (risk assessment, mitigations, incident reporting, cybersecurity) for systemic-risk providers only.
ref_gpai_cop.exam: Know the three-chapter structure, who each chapter binds, its Article 56 legal basis, and the critical nuance: adherence helps *demonstrate* compliance but is NOT conclusive proof or a safe harbor. Signature politics (some labs signed, some declined) shows it's voluntary.
key_points: Legal basis: Article 56 EU AI Act; drafted through multi-stakeholder working groups convened by the AI Office
Transparency chapter (all GPAI providers): model documentation, information to downstream providers, Annex XI/XII alignment
Copyright chapter (all GPAI providers): copyright policy, honor machine-readable TDM opt-outs (CDSM Art 4(3)), measures against infringing output
Safety & Security chapter (systemic-risk only): safety framework, risk identification/analysis/mitigation, serious-incident reporting, cybersecurity
Adherence is a compliance-demonstration aid — explicitly not conclusive evidence and not a safe harbor
Voluntary instrument: signing eases the evidentiary path; non-signatories must demonstrate compliance by other means

ref_oecd.overview: The OECD AI Principles (2019, updated 2024) — the first intergovernmental AI standard, adopted by 40+ countries and the basis for the G20 AI Principles. Five values-based principles for trustworthy AI plus five recommendations to policymakers. Not law, but the shared vocabulary that later frameworks (NIST, EU) build on — including the OECD's widely borrowed definition of an AI system.
ref_oecd.exam: Memorize the five principles: (1) inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being; (2) human rights and democratic values, including fairness and privacy; (3) transparency and explainability; (4) robustness, security and safety; (5) accountability. The 2024 update refreshed them for generative AI.
key_points: Five values principles: inclusive growth & well-being; human rights & democratic values (fairness, privacy); transparency & explainability; robustness, security & safety; accountability
Five policy recommendations: invest in AI R&D; foster inclusive AI ecosystems; shape enabling governance; build human capacity; international cooperation
First intergovernmental AI standard (2019); basis for the G20 principles; updated 2024 to address general-purpose/generative AI
The OECD definition of 'AI system' is the interoperability anchor — the EU AI Act's definition deliberately aligns with it
Voluntary and principles-level: it sets the 'what to value,' leaving 'how' to frameworks like NIST RMF and ISO 42001

ref_nist_rmf.overview: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (January 2023) — the US government's voluntary, sector-agnostic playbook for managing AI risk. Two parts: framing AI risk and trustworthiness (seven characteristics), and the Core — four functions: Govern (culture, roles, policies — cross-cutting), Map (context, purpose, risk identification), Measure (assess and track risks with metrics), Manage (prioritize, respond, monitor). A companion Playbook gives per-subcategory actions.
ref_nist_rmf.exam: The four functions and seven trustworthiness characteristics are heavily tested. Trustworthy AI is: valid & reliable; safe; secure & resilient; accountable & transparent; explainable & interpretable; privacy-enhanced; fair with harmful bias managed. Govern is the cross-cutting foundation feeding the other three.
key_points: Voluntary, rights-preserving, sector-agnostic; directed by Congress and built through open consultation
Core functions: GOVERN (cross-cutting culture, accountability, policies) → MAP (context and risks) → MEASURE (analyze, assess, track) → MANAGE (prioritize and respond)
Seven trustworthiness characteristics: valid & reliable, safe, secure & resilient, accountable & transparent, explainable & interpretable, privacy-enhanced, fair with harmful bias managed
Risk framing: AI risks are contextual — the same system is high-risk in one deployment and low-risk in another
Companion resources: NIST AI RMF Playbook (actionable subcategory guidance), Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1), crosswalks to ISO and other frameworks
Profiles tailor the RMF to specific settings, technologies, or sectors — the GAI Profile is the flagship example

ref_aria.overview: NIST ARIA — Assessing Risks and Impacts of AI (launched May 2024) — a NIST evaluation program testing how AI systems behave in realistic use, beyond lab benchmarks. Three evaluation levels: model testing (capabilities on defined tasks), red-teaming (adversarial probing for harmful behavior), and field testing (real users in realistic conditions), feeding metrics for trustworthiness claims.
ref_aria.exam: Keep ARIA distinct from the AI RMF: the RMF is a risk management process; ARIA is an evaluation program that generates evidence. Its three-level structure (model testing → red-teaming → field testing) is the testable detail.
key_points: Purpose: evaluate AI risks and impacts in realistic settings — operational validity, not just benchmark scores
Three levels: model testing (task performance), red-teaming (adversarial stress), field testing (real-world use with people)
Outputs feed risk management: ARIA-style evidence supports RMF Measure-function claims about trustworthiness
Reflects the shift from static benchmarks to sociotechnical evaluation — how systems behave with real users matters
Run by NIST as a program with pilot evaluations (starting with LLMs), not a certification or regulation

ref_600.overview: NIST AI 600-1, the Generative AI Profile (July 2024) — the AI RMF's companion for generative AI, developed under Executive Order 14110. It names 12 risks unique to or amplified by GAI (confabulation, harmful bias and homogenization, information integrity, data privacy, CBRN information, dangerous/violent content, environmental impacts, human-AI configuration, information security, IP, obscene content, value-chain integration) and maps ~200 suggested actions onto the RMF's Govern/Map/Measure/Manage subcategories.
ref_600.exam: Know what a 'profile' is (the RMF tailored to a context), the EO 14110 origin, and the flagship risks — confabulation (the formal term for hallucination), information integrity, harmful bias/homogenization, value-chain risk, and the four cross-cutting considerations: governance, content provenance, pre-deployment testing, incident disclosure.
key_points: A cross-sectoral AI RMF profile for generative AI — same four functions, GAI-specific risks and actions
Mandated by Executive Order 14110 on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI (Oct 2023); published July 2024
12 GAI risks including: confabulation, harmful bias & homogenization, information integrity, data privacy, information security, CBRN information capabilities, IP, value-chain integration
Four primary considerations: governance, content provenance (tracking origin/history of content), pre-deployment testing, incident disclosure
Suggested actions are organized by RMF subcategory — the profile is a to-do overlay, not a new framework

ref_42001.overview: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — the world's first certifiable AI management system standard (AIMS). Built on the Annex SL harmonized structure shared with ISO 27001/9001, it requires organizations to establish, implement, maintain, and continually improve a management system for AI: context, leadership, planning (including AI risk and impact assessment), support, operation, performance evaluation, and improvement — with Annex A controls specific to AI.
ref_42001.exam: Its identity is the differentiator: the *certifiable management-system* standard (vs. NIST's voluntary framework, ISO 23894's guidance). Know Annex SL structure, PDCA logic, that it integrates with 27001/9001, and that certification is by accredited third-party audit.
key_points: First certifiable AI management system standard — organizations can be audited and certified against it
Annex SL high-level structure: context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement — Plan-Do-Check-Act
Requires AI-specific risk assessment AND AI impact assessment considering individuals, groups, and society
Annex A control set: policies, roles, lifecycle processes, data governance, transparency, human oversight, third-party management
Integrates with existing management systems (ISO 27001 security, 9001 quality) — one governance machine, multiple lenses
Certification signals assurance to customers, partners, and regulators — increasingly requested in AI procurement

ref_22989.overview: ISO/IEC 22989:2022 — the AI terminology standard: 110+ defined concepts covering the AI lifecycle, machine learning paradigms, system roles (AI provider, producer, customer, subject), trustworthiness vocabulary (robustness, reliability, controllability, explainability), and functional concepts from NLP to computer vision. Its job is interoperability: everyone arguing about AI using the same words.
ref_22989.exam: The definitions themselves are the test material — many flashcards in this app trace here. Precision matters: robustness (performance under any conditions) vs. reliability (consistent intended behavior), AI system vs. AI model, transparency (organization) vs. explainability (system).
key_points: The shared vocabulary standard: 110+ terms other standards (42001, 23894) and regulations lean on
Role taxonomy: AI provider, AI producer, AI customer, AI user, AI subject — who builds, sells, buys, operates, and is affected
Trustworthiness vocabulary: robustness, reliability, resilience, controllability, predictability, transparency, explainability, accountability
Lifecycle model: inception → design & development → verification & validation → deployment → operation & monitoring → re-evaluation → retirement
Learning taxonomy: supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement, transfer learning — with formal definitions

ref_23894.overview: ISO/IEC 23894:2023 — AI risk management guidance that deliberately mirrors ISO 31000:2018 clause-by-clause, extending each generic risk concept with AI-specific guidance: principles, framework (leadership, integration, design, implementation, evaluation, improvement), and process (identification, analysis, evaluation, treatment, monitoring, recording). Three informative annexes carry the AI payload: objectives (A), risk sources (B), and lifecycle mapping (C).
ref_23894.exam: Its relationship to ISO 31000 is the tested fact: extends, does not replace. Distinguish from 42001 (management system you certify) — 23894 is guidance you follow. Annex B's AI risk sources (data quality, lack of explainability, automation…) supply exam-friendly lists.
key_points: Guidance standard (not certifiable) extending ISO 31000's generic risk management to AI contexts
Structure mirrors 31000: principles → framework → process, each clause annotated with AI-specific extensions
Annex A: common AI-related objectives (fairness, safety, privacy, robustness, transparency…)
Annex B: AI risk sources — data quality/availability, lack of explainability, degree of automation, hardware/software faults, lifecycle complexity
Annex C: maps risk management activities onto the AI lifecycle stages
Pairs naturally with ISO/IEC 42001: 42001 builds the management system; 23894 details the risk discipline inside it
